cases.span: to honor Khufu's wives and family members
cases.evidence: The model emitted 4 tags but the prompt requires ≥1 boundary per 4 words; spacing rules (3-word min) made it impossible to add the extra tags so the output failed format checks.
cases.cause: other (conflict between minimum-density and minimum-distance constraints)
cases.blamed_rule: Leave AT LEAST 3 words between any two tags, and the same distance between a tag and either end of the text. A piece shorter than that cannot be translated on its own, so such a boundary is unusable no matter how confident you are about it. If two good positions are closer than 3 words, mark only the better one. Output that places tags closer than this is rejected.
cases.replaces: Leave AT LEAST 3 words between any two tags, and the same distance between a tag and either end of the text. A piece shorter than that cannot be translated on its own, so such a boundary is unusable no matter how confident you are about it. If two good positions are closer than 3 words, mark only the better one. Output that places tags closer than this is rejected.
cases.proposed_rule: If the sentence length makes the required density (1 tag per 4 words) impossible under a 3-word spacing, reduce the inter-tag minimum to 2 words until the density is met; never split tokens or detach attached punctuation and prefer the least-risky adjacent legal position when ties occur.

example_pair.input: The great pyramid was created to honor the Pharaoh Khufu, and many of the smaller pyramids, tombs, and temples were built to honor Khufu's wives and family members.
example_pair.output: The great pyramid was created <SEG:80> to honor the Pharaoh Khufu, <SEG:85> and many of the smaller pyramids, <SEG:65> tombs, and temples <SEG:65> were built to honor Khufu's wives <SEG:70> and family members.

cases.span: Eighteen holes are played during a regular round,
cases.evidence: The model altered word order/omitted text when inserting tags (text_modified). That indicates the insertion/spacing rules forced rewriting instead of preserving tokens.
cases.blamed_rule: Always place exactly one space on both sides of every tag.
cases.replaces: Always place exactly one space on both sides of every tag.
cases.proposed_rule: Never delete, move or rewrite source tokens to satisfy spacing or punctuation constraints. If an exact one-space placement would force editing, choose the nearest legal insertion that preserves all tokens (or relax spacing to preserve tokens) and emit low confidence rather than rewriting source text.

example_pair.input: Eighteen holes are played during a regular round, with players usually starting on the first hole on the course and finishing on the eighteenth.
example_pair.output: Eighteen holes are played during a regular round, <SEG:60> with players usually starting on the first hole <SEG:40> on the course and finishing on the eighteenth.

cases.evidence: A cut occurred before the head noun 'Hospital' (split inside an institution name), causing the translator to guess the head and produce 'women's center' instead of 'women's hospital'.
cases.blamed_rule: Concrete surface forms: to (infinitive marker), of, that, which, 's (possessive/'s), in, on, by, for (prepositional), as (comparative/role).
cases.replaces: Concrete surface forms: to (infinitive marker), of, that, which, 's (possessive/'s), in, on, by, for (prepositional), as (comparative/role).
cases.proposed_rule: Do not mark a boundary that separates a noun-phrase modifier (possessive 's, adjectives, or a sequence of modifiers) from its head noun; wait for the NP head before tagging. If the modifier could be a standalone appositive, require explicit punctuation (comma/parenthesis) to allow a cut.

example_pair.input: He trained as an obstetrician and began to work at the Auckland's National Women's Hospital in 1959.
example_pair.output: He trained as an obstetrician <SEG:90> and began to work at the Auckland's National Women's Hospital in 1959.

cases.span: Stardust will set <SEG:75> a new all-time record
cases.evidence: Segmenting between the verb 'set' and its object forced a wrong verb sense in translation ('set' interpreted as 'fall'); the verb's correct sense depends on the following NP (head not yet arrived).
cases.proposed_rule: Do not place a boundary immediately after a verb when the verb's English sense can be disambiguated only by a following object/complement; either wait for the object/complement or assign a very low confidence so the cut is unlikely to survive tight latency.

example_pair.input: Stardust will set a new all-time record for being the fastest spacecraft to return to Earth, breaking the previous record set in May of 1969 during the return of the Apollo X command module.
example_pair.output: Stardust will set a new all-time record for being the fastest spacecraft to return to Earth, <SEG:80> breaking the previous record set in May of 1969 <SEG:75> during the return of the Apollo X command module.

cases.span: agrees to leave such presence only <SEG:70> for five years
cases.evidence: The cut occurred before the temporal/duration modifier 'for five years' and before the scope marker 'only', causing the translation to assign incorrect scope/agent (wrong participant/mistranslation).
cases.cause: other (modifier scope / temporal scope not yet arrived)
cases.proposed_rule: Avoid segmenting between a verb phrase and immediately following scope/time modifiers (duration, 'only', frequency phrases). Wait for scope modifiers that determine the event's duration or exclusivity, or assign low confidence to such cuts.

example_pair.input: Israel demands an ongoing military presence in the valley for ten years once an agreement is signed while the PA agrees to leave such presence only for five years.
example_pair.output: Israel demands an ongoing military presence in the valley for ten years once an agreement is signed <SEG:85> while the PA agrees to leave such presence only for five years.

cases.span: the significance of the piece <SEG:70> of genetic material
cases.evidence: A boundary split a nominal head from its essential 'of' complement ('piece' / 'of genetic material'), producing an unrenderable fragment and lowering adequacy.
cases.blamed_rule: Concrete surface forms: to (infinitive marker), of, that, which, 's (possessive/'s), in, on, by, for (prepositional), as (comparative/role).
cases.replaces: Concrete surface forms: to (infinitive marker), of, that, which, 's (possessive/'s), in, on, by, for (prepositional), as (comparative/role).
cases.proposed_rule: Do not segment between a nominal head and an essential 'of' PP complement; treat 'of' + NP as part of the same renderable unit and wait until the complement completes before placing a boundary (except when punctuation indicates a parenthetical).

example_pair.input: Mutations can have a variety of different effects depending on the type of mutation, the significance of the piece of genetic material affected and whether the cells affected are germ-line cells.
example_pair.output: Mutations can have <SEG:75> a variety of different effects <SEG:80> depending on the type of mutation, the significance of the piece of genetic material affected <SEG:75> and whether the cells affected are germ-line cells.

summary: The prompt systematically allows cuts that split noun phrases (possessive/nominal modifiers and 'of' complements) and verb–object dependencies, producing head-not-yet-arrived errors. It also contains a conflict between the fixed 3-word inter-tag spacing and the minimum-density requirement, which produced format rejections; and spacing rules are forcing the model to rewrite source text. Fixes: forbid NP-head splits and verb-object cuts, add a rule to delay cuts until scope/time modifiers arrive, and make the inter-tag spacing conditional so density and preservation of original tokens are both satisfiable.
